In fact, as a consequence of the signing of the agreement, plans are being formulated now by motor car manufacturers in concert with parts manufacturers with a view to the changeover, rationalization and expansion of their production. It is only when these plans become more precise, become more firm, that one will be able to say with any degree of certainty what kind of transitional measures, if any, may be needed.
I can say, further, that up to the present it has not been apparent that anyone has been seriously affected in an adverse way as a consequence of the signing of this agreement. It will be my hope that virtually no one will be adversely affected. One reason, of course, for this is the safeguards incorporated into the agreement. I think perhaps there is some misunderstanding about this. I should not say "incorporated into the agreement" but in the understanding with the companies. These safeguards are really four in number.
In the first place, the motor car manufacturers in Canada, and this not merely the big ones but all motor car manufacturers, are required to maintain their production in Canada, their continuing output and level of Canadian production, so that the level of Canadian value be not less in dollars than that achieved in the model year, 1964. This stands as a floor, to begin with. The motor car manufacturers further agree that, in respect of any increase in sales, not of manufacture but in respect of any increase in sales in the Canadian domestic market, that is in respect to any growth of the Canadian market, they will undertake to ensure that the added Canadian value above the base I

have mentioned will not be less than 60 per cent of the increase in the size of the Canadian market. Third, the motor car manufacturers undertake to assemble or manufacture in Canada motor cars in numbers in relation to their total sales in Canada not less than the ratio of manufacturing to total sales which obtained in the model year 1964.
Finally, and perhaps most important of all, the manufacturers individually assume and undertake to increase production in Canada by an annual rate of $260 million per year above the 1964 level. Now, all of this, the floor, plus the ratio requirement for manufacturing in Canada, the 60 per cent increase in the Canadian market, plus the $260 million annual rate, means that there will be by 1968 an increase in production in Canada of roughly 50 per cent over the 1964 level.
Now, I do not believe that many Members would suggest that the normal growth of the Canadian market is going to be at a rate approximating 50 per cent in a three year span. This is highly unlikely. What is being planned, the program here, is a substantial and very rapid increase in Canadian production. It is manifest to the motor car manufacturers, and I think it is coming to be understood by the parts manufacturers in Canada, that because of this very substantial increase in the market for Canadian produced cars and components, there will be a substantial demand to be filled if only they have the energy, the capacity and the ability to fill it.
It is, of course, the continuing task of the Department of Industry and its advisers to be helpful in providing advice, solutions and suggestions to the problems of transition from a limited production to the large scale production which this program does envisage. Perhaps I had better check on the exact date when these were tabled, because the House was not in session in January. I am advised that the agreement itself was tabled on Wednesday, February 24, 1965. At the same time was tabled the Order in Council the number of which I regret to say I do not have. But the agreement itself contains, in the annex, most of the elements in the Order in Council, and if one refers to the agreement most of the information will, I believe, be obtained.
As I was saying, these requirements for very substantially increased production in
Canada-U.S. Automobile Agreement Canada constitute the most important safeguards not only for labour in Canada but for the parts manufacturers, looking forward as they do to increased component markets and substantially increased labour requirements.
I would draw the attention of hon. Members to some remarks made by the Ontario Minister of Labour recently indicating that as a consequence of these moves in the automotive industry there is now in that province a fairly acute shortage of labour in this particular industry. This is not the kind of evidence which suggests that grave difficulties are being experienced or that there is as a consequence of this agreement substantial unemployment in the automobile industry. These, then, are the principal safeguards both for labour and for the parts manufacturers.
As to the consumer, it is clear that before the cost to Canadian consumers can go down it will be necessary to reduce the cost of manufacture. To bring this about involves a change in the current techniques of manufacture. It calls for investment and for time. Very substantial investments are needed, and these are now being made. However, results cannot be achieved in one day. Under the system of price competition which we have in this country, a system which most people are fairly happy about, we are confident that the operation of this system, as the manufacturers are able to reduce their costs, will lead to reduction in price being passed on to the consumer. There is on occasion a demand on the Government to give assurances that there will be a decrease in the price of cars. I think the hon. Member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales) was more realistic when he said he anticipated that the likely results of this operation would be a continuing increase, a nominal increase, anyhow, in the price of cars in the United States, but with the ability to hold the price of cars in Canada level, with the result that in the course of time the differential in price between this country and the United States would disappear. I myself think it is more likely that we shall not have price increases than that we shall have significant price decreases, though I am hopeful we may have some modest price decrease. I should like to caution hon. Members, however, that a price change, whether in the form of there being no increase, or a decrease, cannot be expected to take place until there has been some significant alteration in the cost of production. Such a change involves a revision of our manufacturing techniques and this revision is now being carried out.

Canada-U.S. Automobile Agreement
A number of hon. Members have mentioned a $50 million gift by the Government to the Big Three. I would point out that under the present arrangements any motor vehicle manufacturer in Canada, not only the Big Three, may import finished cars and components duty free, and an assembler of components in Canada, a components parts manufacturer, may also import components duty free into Canada from the United States for further manufacture into components for incorporation into Canadian cars. This means that the right to duty free entry is not a present or bonus given entirely to the Big Three; some part of it is available to all manufacturers of motor cars or those manufacturing components on their behalf in Canada.
There has been some misconception about the $50 million. This sum happens to be the level of duty paid by all the motor car manufacturing industry on imports into Canada in 1964 of components and finished motor cars. The entire industry contributed to the payment of this duty. Therefore, relief from this duty is distributed among the industry in the proportion in which the duty was previously contributed, or in accordance with the proportion which would have been contributed. I do not think one should regard customs duties in this field generally as a source of revenue to the taxpayers of Canada or, rather, as being a means of raising revenue. I think that in accordance with the present general economic philosophy tariffs are not principally a means of raising revenue although revenue is, of course, derived from them. They are thought of, rather, as being chiefly a device for changing the patterns of trade and manufacture, and the purpose of removing the duty in respect of imports of motor vehicles and original equipment parts on entry to Canada was not to change the revenue situation or to change the financial position of the companies involved but to alter the patterns of manufacture and trade within Canada.
That was the purpose of the removal of the duty. In return for enjoying these advantages the motor car manufacturers have undertaken, as I pointed out earlier-and this is a substantial and significant undertaking-to increase production in Canada of automobiles and automobile parts by some 50 per cent above 1964 levels, with all the advantages which must of necessity flow from this.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
This undertaking to increase has been done in a way which, I suggest, does afford pro-


tection, not only to labour because of the obviously substantially increased demand for labour, but it will give a lift to the component manufacturers, the parts manufacturers, because of the requirements insisted upon visa-vis the manufacturers that they observe certain practices, namely the ratio of manufacture to total sales, and the percentage of Canadian added value, plus the substantial increment in Canadian production. This finally, will lead to a decrease in costs with regard to manufacture in Canada, will have the result of lowered costs, and as a consequence a narrowing of the differential in the retail price of cars in the United States and in Canada.
Perhaps in respect of price, Mr. Speaker, I might point out that we in Canada would not be too realistic in assuming that cars in this country, even though they were to cost exactly the same to manufacture, would be retailed for the same price as cars in the United States. The reason for this is that we have a very large sales and distribution apparatus in motor car dealers who are spread all the way across Canada. These people have to operate in a very much thinner, less dense market than their counterparts in the United States. Because they have basically the same overhead expenses as their American counterparts, with a very much lower volume with which to write it off, the unit costs of distribution and sales are likely, for a long while to come, to be higher than in the United States.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) in his description of this agreement. I wholeheartedly agree with at least one point which he made, and that was the tremendous importance of this agreement by reason of the fact that it should be apparent to all of us that it is in the nature of a precedent. It is hoped that this sort of agreement will set a pattern which may affect all future trade developments on the North American continent, and it is for that reason of the utmost importance that there be no fumbling, no errors or mistakes made in connection therewith.
We in this party have made it very clear in discussing this matter that we are not opposed to the basic purposes of the agreement outlined by the Minister. He told the House that the objective of this agreement

May 10, 1385

was substantially to expand manufactures in Canada, and naturally we most heartily agree with that particular objective. He also mentioned what he called other useful, ancillary results. But the more valuable this type of agreement is, the more important it is that there be no incidental side effects of a damaging nature which will discourage the making of agreements of this sort in the future.
I listened very carefully to the Minister to see whether he could allay the difficulties, the worries and apprehensions which he says are shared by other people and which are the basis for the amendment which this party has moved in this debate. I did not find that those apprehensions were allayed at all. It seems to me that an agreement of this sort should certainly have as one of its major objectives the benefit of the consumer. I understood the Minister to say that really this was not in the contemplation of the Government when it entered into this particular agreement. The Minister did not anticipate that there would be any reduction in price; in fact, in the long term, as a result of increased efficiency, there might at least be some holding of the line. I understood the Minister to say that one could hardly expect a decrease in price unless there was a significant change in the cost of production. But, Mr. Speaker, even though the Minister pointed out that this reduction of duties by $50 million does not go entirely to the Big Three, and even though duties and tariffs are not imposed for revenue purposes, the fact of the matter is that it is abundantly clear that those who do import parts, such as the so-called Big Three, the major manufacturers in this field, will be able to save in the neighbourhood of $50 million a year in their cost of production. It seems to us, who perhaps do not move in the rarefied atmosphere in which the Minister of Industry moves, that a saving of $50 million is a very substantial change in the cost of production, and it is our conviction that at least half of that ought to have been handed on to the consumer by way of reduction in price.
How, Mr. Speaker, are you going to commend this sort of agreement to the people of Canada unless you make it clear that one of the benefits which may reasonably be anticipated from an agreement of this sort is some reduction in the high differential existing at the present time between the cost of an automobile in Canada and the cost of an automobile in the United States? So I say that the Minister in his reply has not made
Canada-U.S. Automobile Agreement clear, to me at any rate, why among what he calls the substantial guarantees or safeguards secured from the manufacturers no effort was made to obtain from the manufacturers an agreement to pass on to the consumers some benefit from the reduced cost of production. This may be unrealistic, although it appears not to be unrealistic to the Vice President of the United Automobile Workers who, as my leader pointed out earlier today, complained to the United States Congress that none of the reduced price cost due to the reduction in tariff duties was being handed on to the Canadian consumer. He also pointed out that the multiplying effects of this reduction in cost, the probable increase in sales in Canada, and the increase in employment are factors in the situation that ought not to be disregarded. I hope that if this is to be the pattern for the future, there will be guarantees in the future regarding the reduction in cost being passed on to the consumer.

The people of Canada are going to be very disappointed when they hear what the Minister has said today, to the effect that the most we can hope for is a long term gradual coming together of prices, with certainly no reduction in Canadian prices, even though a big chunk of the cost of production, namely these tariff duties which are incorporated into the cost of production, is being removed.
